narration: Toys R Us. Sears. Payless. Red Lobster. RadioShack. Beloved brands you grew up with — all dead, or barely breathing. And a surprising number share one hidden cause of death.
caption: beloved brands — all dead

narration: It usually wasn't Amazon that killed them. It wasn't even that people stopped loving them. In case after case, they were quietly loaded up with debt — and bled dry — by their own owners.
So when you hear a chain 'just couldn't compete anymore,' hold that thought. Often it was never given a fair chance to.
The owner, almost every time, is the same kind of creature. A private equity firm.
And these firms are now enormous. They've quietly bought up restaurants, retailers, hospitals, newspapers — even the houses people rent.
And here's the twist that makes people furious. The brand can die — and the firm that killed it still walks away richer.
This isn't a fringe story. Private-equity-owned companies now employ millions of people — and they go bankrupt at far higher rates than normal firms.
So let's open up the private equity playbook — and see exactly how a profitable company gets turned into a corpse, at a profit.
heading: How Private Equity Kills Your Favorite Brands
sub: The company dies. The firm gets paid.

narration: Private equity now manages trillions of dollars and owns companies employing a huge chunk of the American workforce. This machine touches almost everyone.
Start with what private equity even is. It's ownership of companies that aren't listed on the public stock market.
A private equity firm raises a giant fund — mostly from pensions and endowments — and uses it to buy entire companies.
The pitch to the public is noble: we buy struggling companies, make them better and leaner, and everyone wins. Sometimes, genuinely, that happens.
The brochure says 'we rescue and improve companies.' The playbook, too often, says something very different.
memeBottom: we extract the cash and leave

narration: But the real magic trick is how they buy. Because they barely use their own money at all.
The tool is the leveraged buyout — buying a company using a large amount of borrowed money.
A typical deal: the firm puts in a small slice of its own cash, and borrows the rest — often the great majority of the purchase price.
caption: a little cash, a lot of debt

narration: And now the part that sounds made up, but is completely real. The debt used to buy the company… gets put on the company's own books.
Imagine buying a house with someone else's mortgage — and then making the house itself responsible for the payments. That's a leveraged buyout.
caption: the company carries the debt

narration: So on day one, a healthy company suddenly owes a fortune it never borrowed, to fund its own purchase. Its margin for error just vanished.

You might wonder why any lender hands over billions for this. Because the loans pay juicy interest — and the lenders quickly sell that debt on to other investors, so they rarely hold the risk themselves.
It's other people's money, all the way down. The firm risks little of its own. The lenders pass on the danger. And the company is left holding every bit of it.
Now the company is owned, and buried in debt. Here's how the firm extracts its profit — whether or not the company survives.
heading: The Extraction Playbook

narration: Trick one: the fees. The firm charges the company management and 'monitoring' fees — getting paid every year, just for owning it.
On top of that, the partners keep a big slice of any profits — the famous 'carried interest.'
So the firm is paid fees for owning it, and a cut of any gains. Already, it makes money whether the company thrives or not.
Trick two is the one that stuns people: the dividend recapitalization.
The firm makes the company borrow even more money — and then pays that fresh cash straight to itself, as a dividend.
caption: borrow more → pay yourself

narration: Read that again. They don't put money in. They make the company take on new debt, and hand them the proceeds. The firm can recover its entire investment this way — while leaving the company even deeper in the hole.

In the most brazen deals, firms pull out more in dividends than they ever put in — sometimes within a year or two — making the trade risk-free for themselves before the company's fate is even decided.
Once the firm has its money back, it almost doesn't matter what happens next. Heads it wins big; tails it already cashed out.
caption: de-risked before the story ends

narration: Trick three: sell what the company owns, and rent it back. The sale-and-leaseback.
If the company owns its stores or warehouses, the firm sells that real estate, pockets the cash — and the company now has to pay rent, forever, on buildings it used to own.
caption: sell the building, pay rent forever

narration: In one move, a huge asset is converted into cash for the owner — and a permanent new bill for the company. Short-term gain, long-term bleed.
Trick four, when the others have run their course, is the oldest one of all: asset stripping.
Sell off the brands, the inventory, the patents, the land — anything of value — and carry the proceeds out the door. What's left is a husk that still owes money.
caption: strip the value, leave the husk

narration: And to service all that debt, the company slashes costs. Layoffs. Lower quality. Squeezed suppliers. Deferred investment. The things customers loved, quietly gutted.
The customer feels it first — as the exact things that made the brand special quietly disappear.
memeBottom: cutting the stuff customers actually loved

narration: This all sounds abstract. So let's watch it kill a company you probably remember. Toys R Us.
heading: Case One: Toys R Us

narration: In 2005, a group of private equity firms bought Toys R Us for about six and a half billion dollars.
caption: 2005: bought for $6.6B

narration: Most of that price was borrowed — leaving the company saddled with around five billion dollars of debt it had never chosen to take on.
sub: of debt loaded onto Toys R Us

narration: The interest alone ate hundreds of millions a year — money that could have gone into stores, staff, and fighting back against Amazon and Walmart.
So while rivals invested in websites and experiences, Toys R Us was stuck making debt payments. It wasn't out-competed so much as financially handcuffed.
caption: handcuffed by debt, not beaten by Amazon

narration: In 2017, Toys R Us filed for bankruptcy. Around thirty-three thousand workers eventually lost their jobs — many at first with no severance at all.
Meanwhile, the firms had collected fees for over a decade. The workers got pink slips. The owners got paid. That contrast is the entire story.
When Toys R Us collapsed, workers were initially offered nothing in severance. Only a public outcry forced the firms to set up a modest hardship fund.
And here's the cruelest irony. Some of the pensions that funded these buyouts belonged to workers whose own jobs the deals later destroyed. Their savings quietly bet against their paychecks.
If you think that's a one-off, meet a more recent victim — from your dinner table. Red Lobster.
heading: Case Two: Red Lobster

narration: Red Lobster's problem wasn't really seafood. A big part of it was a classic sale-and-leaseback of the very ground its restaurants sat on.
Its valuable real estate was sold off for a one-time cash windfall — and suddenly the chain had to pay rent on hundreds of locations it used to own outright.
caption: its own land, sold out from under it

narration: That permanent rent bill turned manageable restaurants into money-losers. The cushion that lets a business survive a bad year was simply gone.
Then came the infamous 'endless shrimp' deal — an all-you-can-eat promotion that bled money as costs rose. A desperate grab for sales, by a company with no room to absorb a mistake.
In 2024, Red Lobster filed for bankruptcy. The seafood was a scapegoat. The financial engineering was the real cause.
The headlines blamed shrimp. The balance sheet told the real story.
memeBottom: it wasn't the shrimp — it was the rent

narration: And it is a very long list. Payless. Sears. Friendly's. Mervyn's. Fairway. Brand after brand, run through the exact same machine.
caption: the same playbook, again and again

narration: Each time, the headlines reach for an easy villain — Amazon, the internet, changing tastes. Underneath, the same debt-and-extraction engine kept quietly running.
So why does this keep happening? Because of one beautiful, brutal asymmetry.
heading: Heads I Win, Tails You Lose

narration: The firm plays with very little of its own money. The rest is debt the company owes, and cash from outside investors.

So if the company thrives, the firm makes a fortune on the upside. If it dies, the firm has often already pulled its money out through fees and dividends — and it's the company's lenders and workers who eat the loss.
caption: upside theirs, downside yours

narration: A favorite move is the 'roll-up' — buy dozens of small firms in one industry, bolt them together, strip out staff, raise prices, and sell the giant for a markup.
At its most extreme, this is simply asset stripping — selling a company for parts to boost returns for the financial owners.
And who's on the hook for the losses? Often the pension funds that invested in the PE fund — which can mean, indirectly, ordinary workers' retirement savings.
The suppliers who go unpaid. The towns that lose their biggest employer. The customers who lose a brand they loved. The costs are spread everywhere — the profits, concentrated in a few.
And the damage doesn't stop at the company gates. When a town's biggest employer is stripped and shuttered, the local shops, suppliers and tax base can collapse right along with it.
There's even a tax twist. The partners' cut of the profits — that carried interest — is often taxed at a lower rate than ordinary wages. The extraction is quietly subsidized.
Fail the company, keep the fees, and pay a discount rate on the winnings. It's a remarkably good deal — for exactly one party.
memeBottom: the tax code: here's a discount

narration: Now, in fairness — because this gets ranty fast — private equity is not pure villainy.
heading: To Be Fair

narration: Sometimes a struggling company genuinely needs new owners, hard decisions, and fresh capital. Plenty of PE deals do create real, lasting value.
The problem isn't buying companies. It's a model where the owner can get rich even when the company fails — because that quietly rewards extraction over building.
When failure still pays, you shouldn't be shocked that failure keeps happening.
And it's spreading to places that really matter. Private equity now owns hospitals, nursing homes, and vet clinics — where cutting costs to service debt can mean cutting actual care.
Researchers have linked some private-equity nursing-home takeovers to worse outcomes for residents. When this playbook meets human care, the stakes stop being about toys.
So what do you actually take from this — as a customer, a worker, or an investor?
heading: What to Watch For

narration: As a customer, watch for the tells. A long-loved brand suddenly cuts corners, raises prices, closes stores, and feels hollowed out. That's often a balance sheet talking, not a boardroom losing its touch.
As a worker, know that a private equity takeover often means the clock is ticking — on jobs, on investment, and on the company's independence.
Remember the four moves. Load it with debt. Charge it fees. Borrow more to pay yourself. Sell its assets and rent them back. Then cut costs to survive the wreckage.
lines: 4. sell its assets, rent them back

narration: Do all that, and a company that was perfectly healthy can be bled into bankruptcy — while the people who did it were paid, handsomely, the entire time.
caption: healthy company, engineered death

narration: Because in this game, the company's survival was never really the goal. The fees, the dividends, and the asset sales were. The brand was just the raw material.
It even owns a fast-growing share of single-family rental homes now — applying the very same squeeze to tenants that it once applied to toy stores.
So the next time a brand you grew up with quietly dies, don't just assume it 'couldn't keep up.' Ask who owned it — and how much they made on the way down.
Because in this game, a dead company isn't a failure. It's just the final, fully-extracted stage of a very successful trade.
caption: a 'successful' deal can still kill the company
